#2085. Why must Manchester United move beyond the Glazers?

Shumail Sajid writes about Manchester United for Read Man Utd and Crystal Palace for Read Crystal Palace, with occasional pieces on other Premier League clubs. He has also written for FanSided's Red Devils Dispatch, Yardbarker, Anfield Central and The Sports Side.

The Glazers took control of Manchester United in 2005. That takeover has since caused so many disruptions and protests by the fans over massive debts and insufficient backing of the team in the transfer market, despite successful periods in the Premier League and Europe.

Now Manchester United need to think about who should control the club in the future. Laurie Whitwell has now shared his views on why Manchester United need an ownership change. He simply wants the Glazers gone from Old Trafford. However, he also recognizes that replacing the current ownership doesn’t automatically mean things will improve for United.

The journalist believes the change in ownership has had a lasting effect on United, with the club still feeling its consequences today. A fresh start might be welcome, but the identity of the next owners would matter just as much as the departure of the existing ones.

“Personally, I would like to see the Glazers gone from Manchester United,” Laurie Whitwell said on The Rest is Football podcast with Gary Lineker.

“That change, you know, just really affected and still impacts United now.”

The desire for different ownership is one thing, but finding people capable of taking the club forward is another.

Whitwell admitted there is no perfect answer when it comes to who should take charge.

That leaves United facing a difficult choice. A sale could offer the chance to change how the club is run, but simply bringing in a new owner would not guarantee better decisions or a brighter future.

Whitwell also raised the idea of United supporters having a greater say in the club’s ownership and decisions, much like the Barcelona model where fans own the club itself. However, he highlighted that the Barcelona model isn’t ideal either and has its own shortcomings.

Changing the names at the top would only be one part of the change. The club would also need an ownership structure capable of making sound decisions and providing a direction.

The issue of ownership goes beyond whether the Glazers should stay or leave. Manchester United needs to find the right people and the right model to secure the club’s future. Getting that decision wrong could leave them facing the same circus the fans are enduring under the Glazers.

#2084. Arsenal’s Havertz penalty controversy sparks fresh call for change to football laws

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Arsenal’s controversial penalty claim against Hull City has raised new questions about how the offside rule is interpreted in football.

Former Premier League official Dermot Gallagher believes that whilst he understands why the officials made the decision, the result would have been different under the current rules.

Speaking on Ref Watch on Sky Sports, Gallagher said that the holding should have been the main focus of the incident involving Kai Havertz and Hull defender Nobel Mendy.

His comments have increased criticism of referee Farai Hallam and VAR official Michael Oliver. However, Gallagher also feels that the language used in the laws needs to be addressed to avoid this issue in the future.

The incident happened shortly before half-time during Arsenal’s 1-0 victory over Hull at the Emirates Stadium.

Mendy pulled Havertz’s shirt inside the penalty area, prompting VAR to recommend an on-field review. Hallam subsequently confirmed that the Hull defender had committed a holding offence.

However, he ruled that Havertz was in an offside position and awarded Hull a free-kick.

Gallagher believes that was incorrect under the laws of the game. He explained that being in an offside position does not automatically constitute an offence.

The player must be involved in play before the referee can give a penalty. In this instance, Havertz had not tried to play the ball or challenge an opponent before being pulled back by Mendy.

This means that the player was held first, so a penalty should have been given to Arsenal.

Gallagher said that the AR had first raised their flag for offside. He said that it was a great process with VAR, but the initial decision could have affected the outcome.

He recognised why the decision was made even though he felt Arsenal should have been awarded the penalty.

In terms of common sense, he said it does not look right to award the penalty, as Havertz was in an offside position and couldn’t legally contest for the ball.

But he emphasised that the officials must strictly enforce the laws of the game. Gallagher thinks there is some grey space here which can be addressed by having more specific wording.

This could be crucial in these types of situations as the difference between being in an offside position and committing an offside offence can have a big effect on whether a penalty is awarded.

It’s a small comfort for Arsenal after missing the chance to take the lead from the spot. But Martin Odegaard did eventually score the winner in the 72nd minute to give Mikel Arteta’s men three points.

The incident has exposed a wider problem for referees. Until the laws provide clearer guidance, similar decisions could continue to generate controversy.

#2082. Bolton Wanderers fans will love what James Trafford said after England heroics v Spain

England became the first team to beat Spain since March 2024 on Sunday night, topping Group C of the Nations League, due in no small part to Leeds United goalkeeper James Trafford. But even that double save at the end doesn't top one effort while at Bolton Wanderers.

The Three Lions weathered quite the storm in the final half hour, despite cruising at 3-0 thanks to goals from Harry Kane, Esri Konsa and Ben White.

A lapse in concentration let Lamine Yamal nick the ball and race away, and a second error seconds later saw Elliot Anderson drag the Spaniard down in the box, giving away a penalty and earning a straight red.

But despite Spain halving the deficit after converting the spot kick, England saw out the win, with Trafford proving to be the hero between the sticks. He made six saves, including a brilliant double stop at the end to deny Yamal and then Aymeric Laporte.

An incredible moment, and one that, for 99% of goalkeepers, would be the pinnacle of their careers thus far. Not for Trafford, though.

Trafford first made a name for himself as one of England's most exciting young goalkeepers while on loan at Bolton from Manchester City. He spent the second half of the 2021/22 campaign at the Toughsheet Stadium, but really broke through the following year.

The 24-year-old kept 22 clean sheets for the Trotters en route to the play-offs, making plenty of big saves to help what was then Ian Evatt's side save points, while also failing to concede in any of his four EFL Trophy matches as Bolton won at Wembley against Plymouth Argyle.

His second clean sheet back in a Wanderers shirt came at Port Vale, and despite it being over four years ago, he hasn't seemed to forget it.

FLW has debated which 15 fanbases generate the best atmospheres and more inside their home stadiums

Speaking to ITV after the win over Spain, Trafford was asked if that double save to deny Yamal and Laporte was "as good as he's made," and after thinking about it, the 24-year-old had to disagree.

"The moment's a brilliant moment," he said. "As in saves, I made an incredible one away at Port Vale when I was at Bolton, and that will forever be my best save. But for the moment, what it meant, yeah, it's up there."

The game ended 0-0 at Vale Park, and you'll be hard-pressed to find a fan of either side who remembers much about what happened, but that one moment will live in the goalkeeper's head for the rest of his career.

It's the old moniker, 'never fall in love with a loan player,' but it seems that the love is still mutual between Trafford and Bolton, even though his departure was over three years ago now.

As seen above, it's quite a brilliant save, and while Trafford and the Bolton fans had some brilliant memories after that third game of the campaign at Port Vale, those in the stands at the Toughsheet will love their mention after one of the best performances of the 24-year-old's life.

"I made an incredible [save] away at Port Vale when I was at Bolton" Our boy 🤍 we love you," one Bolton fan commented under the interview online. "Our boy james Trafford, loves Bolton and Bolton love him !!" was also among the comments, as was "He loves bolton . He always does."

"Makes a world-class double save to help England beat the world champions, but still puts another above it - Bolton away at Port Vale in League One. Never change!" a Bolton fan account tweeted.

"Hahahaha I love him England vs Spain? Yeah big moment, but fav save? For Bolton vs Port Vale 😂," was also commented. Trafford's matter-of-fact and somewhat unconventional interview style does lend well to some fans, especially those at Bolton, who will have immense pride towards their former loanee keeper.

Trafford is one of the prime examples of how EFL loans can help shape a player and ready them for big things in their career. The fact that the 24-year-old was playing in League One just four seasons ago is quite something.

Now, the Leeds number one is arguably one of the best goalkeepers in the Premier League, and after that performance against Spain, the number one elect for England, according to some fans.

What current English EFL loanees do you think will make the step up into England contention in the future? Let us know in the comments.

A club's fanbase can often take pride in a former loanee going on to big things and, in this case, Bolton fans won't be letting the footballing world forget that Trafford was in their squad not that long ago.

From this, though, it seems that the 24-year-old himself isn't going to let people forget his time at the Toughsheet Stadium, either.

Shumail Sajid writes about Manchester United for Read Man Utd and Crystal Palace for Read Crystal Palace, with occasional pieces on other Premier League clubs. He has also written for FanSided's Red Devils Dispatch, Yardbarker, Anfield Central and The Sports Side.

The Argentinian defender has also apologized to the United higher ups as well over his comments, as shared by Fabrizio Romano.

Lisandro Martinez has held discussions with Jason Wilcox and Michael Carrick after speaking out following United’s 2-0 defeat to Atletico Madrid.

Martinez had questioned whether Carrick was backed enough in the summer and suggested the club needed changes.

Fabrizio Romano has now confirmed that United consider the matter resolved for now and expect Martinez to remain available for selection.

Speaking about the situation on his YouTube channel, as quoted by Football 365, Romano explained why Martinez’s comments caused concern inside the club.

“He spoke very strongly after the game against Atletico Madrid, which Man Utd lost. It was a very negative moment for the Red Devils. We know that Licha was very strong in his comments. He said that Michael Carrick was not backed enough during the summer transfer window.”

Romano added that Martinez had spoken directly to those at the club after the incident.

“Licha apologised to Man Utd as a club. He spoke to the directors, he spoke to Jason Wilcox, and he spoke to Michael Carrick, who was also involved in this conversation.”

“So, the underlying message remains the same. Lisandro is apologising for the way he expressed himself after a game during a difficult moment for Man Utd, but there was a discussion about the substance of what he said.”

Romano also revealed that United had imposed a financial penalty on the centre-back. However, the punishment does not appear to involve removing him from the squad.

“According to the information available tonight, Lisandro Martinez has been fined.”

He added that Martinez is expected to return to the squad as normal, with the fine considered sufficient punishment for the incident.

#2077. Why fresh £70m Middlesbrough update will spark interest at Blackburn Rovers

The end of the calendar year is approaching, which means so is the January transfer window, and Championship clubs will be bracing for interest in some of the better-performing players in the division.

All eyes are on Middlesbrough at the moment, and how much interest they'll face for Will Lankshear, who only just joined the Teessiders this past summer in a deal which could break their transfer record.

As it stands, that potential £20 million fee may not be fully paid, as the 21-year-old has showcased his Premier League quality in the few months he's spent at the Riverside, and his potential is something that elite top-flight sides are keen to invest in.

Middlesbrough will be doing their best to scare off any potential suitors this January with a hefty price tag, but in the wake of their reported asking price, it raises the question of how much other clubs should demand for their big-hitters; more specifically, how much Blackburn Rovers should demand for Andri Gudjohnsen.

There was plenty of expectation surrounding Lankshear ahead of this season. The 21-year-old was still very highly rated out of the Tottenham Hotspur academy, hitting headlines after he scored and then was sent off in a Europa League defeat at Galatasaray in November 2024.

He'd also scored 12 in all competitions last year for an Oxford United side that was relegated from the Championship, with it almost universally agreed that he was a big bright spark in an otherwise disappointing campaign for the Yellows.

However, not many expected Lankshear to be this good, this soon, at his new club. The 21-year-old has 15 goals in 16 games in all competitions for Boro, including 13 in 13 Championship games.

The Middlesbrough frontman has been the clinical focal point that Kim Hellberg needed in his side, and it's evident through their lack of goals after he picked up a small hamstring issue how important he is to this Boro side.

Due to these performances, though, the likes of Arsenal, Manchester United and other Premier League sides are reportedly keen on his services as soon as this January. In response, the Sun reported that Middlesbrough have slapped a £70 million price tag on his head.

He wouldn't be the most expensive Championship departure if that did go through - West Ham United somehow managed to get £85 million for Mateus Fernandes this past summer - but it's an eyebrow-raising demand, and an equal indication that Lankshear is not for sale without blatantly outlining that.

Blackburn may be looking at the news regarding Middlesbrough's price tag for Lankshear and wonder why they can't adopt a similar approach as and when interest forms for their talisman, Andri Gudjohnsen.

Of the players who have played 750 minutes or more in the Championship this season, Lankshear and Gudjohnsen stand atop the goals-per-90 charts. The Boro man averages 1.12, while the Icelandic forward sits at 0.96. There's a sizable drop to Jack Moylan in third with 0.70.

Which fanbases can improve on their current atmosphere offerings? The computer has had its say....

Unlike the 21-year-old, though, Gudjohnsen hasn't needed a plethora of chances to score his goals, as Blackburn don't have the quality behind the striker as Middlesbrough does. Indeed, Lankshear has taken 28 more shots — more than double the Rovers man so far this season.

Gudjohnsen stands out due to his sheer prolific nature infront of goal. He has 10 this season from just 20 shots; a 50% conversion rate, which makes him the most clinical player in Europe.

Lankshear is important to Middlesbrough, but, arguably, Gudjohnsen at this stage is more crucial to Blackburn. If clubs come calling in January, Rovers need to be firm with their demands for the 24-year-old.

Ultimately, Middlesbrough's demands when it comes to a fee for Lankshear are heavily influenced by 'English tax.' English clubs always demand that little bit more, or in this case, a lot more, for home-grown domestic players.

Gudjohnsen isn't that, but instead, he comes with a marketable name that not many in his position have.

Collect every point to win the round. Don’t let Neil Warnock catch you.

Arrow keys or WASD to move. P to pause, M to mute.

Swipe on the pitch or use the pad to move.

The 24-year-old is a third-generation star, and both his grandfather and father were legends in Icelandic football. His Dad, Eidur, made quite a name for himself in England and Spain, too, winning a couple of Premier League titles with Chelsea and being part of the treble-winning Barcelona side under Pep Guardiola in 2008/09.

That kind of heritage is incredibly marketable. It'll make Icelandic fans follow their club and will draw eyes towards them to see how an Icelandic legend's son is performing in a big Premier League side.

Blackburn can use the Gudjohnsen name to their advantage to add a few more millions to the price tag to almost counteract the lack of homegrown status.

Ultimately, that £70 million price tag for Lankshear is a way to scare off suitors, and Blackburn should be doing the same. They aren't under any pressure to sell Gudjohnsen, given he signed a new "long-term" deal just last May.

How much do you think Andri Gudjohnsen is worth right now? Let us know in the comments.

The 24-year-old has showcased that this club form isn't just a fluke, netting a hat-trick for Iceland in their Nations League win over Bulgaria last Friday, and will return to Ewood Park looking to continue this momentum.

If he maintains this clinical nature in front of goal, Rovers could emerge as late play-off contenders as the campaign goes on. At the very least, it will attract further suitors in the summer, and Gudjohnsen's price tag could be even higher by then.

It may not be as lucrative as a £70 million fee, but Blackburn should be getting a little excited over how much they could earn from a Gudjohnsen sale in the future.

#2075. Chelsea World Cup Knockout Load Gives Xabi Alonso Pre-Season Problem

Chelsea’s World Cup contingent has moved from a group-stage watchlist into a genuine Xabi Alonso planning problem.

Chelsea’s own tournament update confirms that Enzo Fernandez, Mike Penders, Moises Caicedo, Kendry Paez, Malo Gusto and Jorrel Hato have reached the Round of 32.

England have also progressed after their final Group L win over Panama, which keeps Reece James and Trevoh Chalobah inside the wider knockout picture.

For supporters, that is a status marker. For Alonso, it is where summer pride starts to become pre-season compression.

The concern is not simply volume. It is where the minutes are landing.

Enzo has not missed a minute for Argentina, while Caicedo has remained central for Ecuador and captained them in the 2-1 win over Germany.

Those are not fringe workloads. They are the two midfield profiles Chelsea have built large parts of their control game around.

Alonso’s first Chelsea pre-season was always going to demand clarity through the middle of the pitch.

Instead, the players most central to that reset are still operating in knockout football.

Caicedo’s Ecuador role is the cleanest example. Read Chelsea has already assessed how his captaincy display against Germany strengthened his leadership case, but the next layer is more complicated.

Every additional knockout tie gives him more tournament rhythm, more authority and more fatigue.

Argentina’s route against Cape Verde keeps him on a glamorous stage at exactly the moment Chelsea need to settle his role, mood and tactical responsibilities under Alonso.

If Madrid-related noise continues around him, the club cannot afford a sluggish July handover.

Reece James started England’s first two matches before a hamstring issue ruled him out of the Panama game, according to the Guardian.

England still topped the group and moved into a last-32 tie with DR Congo, but James’ situation is exactly the kind of detail Chelsea’s medical team will monitor closely.

Chelsea have already had to plan around a large World Cup group.

The broader issue was clear in Read Chelsea’s earlier pre-season workload piece, but the knockout stage sharpens it because the returns will now be staggered.

Enzo brings a maximum group-stage load. Caicedo brings captaincy responsibility and heavy Ecuador minutes.

James brings knockout qualification mixed with another hamstring-management question.

Gusto and Hato remain tied to France and the Netherlands, while Penders and Paez are still absorbing tournament environments before club reintegration.

That is a spine issue, not a fringe issue.

Alonso needs automatisms in possession, spacing around the double pivot, clearer full-back behaviour and pressing triggers from midfield.

Those details do not bed in properly when key players arrive in drips after a major summer tournament.

Players returning from knockout football can bring competitive sharpness that closed-door friendlies cannot replicate.

Caicedo captaining Ecuador through pressure games matters. Enzo playing high-leverage minutes for Argentina matters.

Gusto and Hato absorbing tournament detail also helps Chelsea’s defensive reset.

But Chelsea cannot treat every tournament minute as clean preparation.

Alonso must decide who returns straight into tactical work, who needs a genuine pause and who can handle August without creating an avoidable injury bill by September.

That is where the James situation feels central.

If Chelsea’s captain carries a World Cup hamstring warning, the club’s right-sided structure becomes more than a selection debate.

It becomes an availability question that touches Gusto, the wider defensive rebuild and the need for control from midfield.

Read Chelsea has already looked at James’ captaincy test under Alonso, and the injury layer now makes that test sharper.

This is the hidden cost of a strong international footprint.

Chelsea want players good enough to survive deep into tournaments.

Alonso now has to make sure that status does not leave his first league weeks short of the very control those players are meant to provide.

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

There is no breathing space for the Arsenal squad. 19 players are going to represent their countries in international fixtures in the final break of 2026. Many will face crucial moments in the coming days with Nations League promotions and relegations still at stake.

There are plenty of important fixtures in November. A number of Arsenal players will be looking to help their countries qualify for the Nations League quarter-finals. However, whilst others will be battling to avoid relegation. A number of Gunners will also be facing their club teammates in some interesting fixtures.

One of the biggest matches will be the clash between England and Spain on November 15th in Madrid.

Spain includes David Raya, Martin Zubimendi and Mikel Merino in their squad, meaning they could face five Arsenal teammates. Declan Rice, Eberechi Eze, Ben White, Myles Lewis-Skelly and Ezri Konsa are all in Thomas Tuchel’s England squad.

Spain lead England by three points in their Nations League group, but the Lionesses have a chance to keep their quarter-final hopes alive if they can defeat Croatia at Wembley on November 12.

Konsa will be absent during the first match as he undertakes personal training, but he could return in time for the encounter against Spain.

There is more Arsenal interest in Group A2. Jurrien Timber’s Netherlands facing Christos Tzolis’ Greece on November 13, followed by a clash with Kai Havertz’s Germany three days later.

Both the Netherlands and Greece are tied on eight points. Germany will be looking to move up in the standings against Serbia.

These games could affect how a number of Arsenal players come back into the fold with such a busy run of fixtures.

Viktor Gyokeres has the chance to help Sweden move up to League A.

The forward has scored four goals in four Nations League games. Sweden are two points clear at the top of their group. A win against Bosnia and Herzegovina on November 14 will guarantee them a promotion.

They then head to Poland for their final game. Gyokeres will be looking to continue his goal scoring and return to Arsenal with confidence.

However, Martin Odegaard will have a tough task ahead. Norway currently sit bottom of their group having only picked up three points from four games.

With three points behind second place Denmark, Norway will host Wales before heading to Denmark on November 17. Both games will be crucial for the Norwegians to avoid relegation.

Riccardo Calafiori will be on duty for Italy against France and Belgium. Piero Hincapie has two friendly matches against Ecuador, one against Costa Rica and one against Bolivia.

Bruno Guimaraes and Gabriel Magalhaes will be travelling to play against Japan and Singapore with Brazil. Kepa Arrizabalaga has received his first call-up to the Basque squad for their friendly against Venezuela.

James Scanlon could have a successful campaign with Gibraltar. Two wins against Andorra and Malta would see them top their group and progress to League C.

With so many Arsenal players playing in competitive matches, the international break could have an impact on a number of countries. Mikel Arteta will be hoping his players return in good condition before they resume their domestic campaign.

#2073. Leeds vs Man Utd preview: Team news, form, injuries and where to watch

Shumail Sajid writes about Manchester United for Read Man Utd and Crystal Palace for Read Crystal Palace, with occasional pieces on other Premier League clubs. He has also written for FanSided's Red Devils Dispatch, Yardbarker, Anfield Central and The Sports Side.

Leeds United welcome Manchester United to Elland Road on Sunday, with both sides looking to put a difficult run of results behind them and get their Premier League season on track.

Leeds United suffered a 2-1 defeat away to Arsenal last weekend despite James Justin scoring to put them in front in the 55th minute.

Manchester United also dropped points in the Premier League, drawing 1-1 with Tottenham, before losing 2-0 to Atletico Madrid in the Champions League away from home.

Michael Carrick’s side have struggled to find consistency in recent weeks and have come under immense pressure to get in results. The Whites meanwhile will hope that home advantage can make the difference when United face their bitter rivals on Elland Road.

Leeds have recorded one win, two draws and two defeats in their last five matches in all competitions. Their best result came against Newcastle, where they won, but a 6-3 defeat to Chelsea in the Carabao Cup and the loss to Arsenal have left them searching for a response.

Manchester United have also won just once in their last five matches. Their 4-0 Champions League victory over Sabah FK was the only comfortable win, but defeats to Manchester City and Atletico Madrid, alongside draws against Fulham and Tottenham, have raised questions about their form and Michael Carrick.

Leeds are waiting on Dan James, who returned from international duty with a back problem and missed the Arsenal game. Joe Rodon remains sidelined with a hamstring injury and is not expected back in full training until next month. Harry Wilson could return after being an unused substitute last weekend. Mateo Joseph is also among Leeds’ absentees.

Manchester United have their own concerns. Luke Shaw and Kobbie Mainoo are doubts after picking up issues against Tottenham and missing Tuesday’s trip to Madrid. Benjamin Sesko remains unavailable with a recurring shin problem, while Patrick Dorgu is expected to be out until late November. Manuel Ugarte is recovering from knee surgery, and Noussair Mazraoui is a doubt with a back problem.

There is better news regarding Matthijs de Ligt, who could return to contention. Leny Yoro is also available for selection despite his Champions League suspension.

The match takes place at Elland Road on Sunday, October 18. Kick-off is scheduled for 2 pm BST (1pm GMT).

UK viewers can watch the game live on Sky Sports Main Event, with coverage beginning at 1 pm BST.

#2072. Top 8 most famous footballers to ever play in the EFL Championship (Ranked)

The Championship is a fantastic league when it comes to producing talent, with many of Thomas Tuchel’s England squad having featured at this level in the past.

The competitive nature of the second tier, combined with the technical and physical demands it places on players, mean it’s a relentless division that will test individuals in different ways.

Some struggle to cope with that, although others flourish, and it can be the perfect environment for young players to show what they can do.

However, it’s not just up-and-coming players who enjoy the Championship, as some of the biggest names in the game have turned out in England’s second division in the past.

Football League World has asked AI to predict the 2027/28 EFL Championship table if Manchester United and Manchester City were in it

With that in mind, FLW has ranked the EIGHT most famous footballers to have played in the Championship, even if they weren’t necessarily the best…

The 39-year-old is a Leicester City legend, with the high point of his career coming when he helped the Foxes to the Premier League title.

Many people love Vardy for his rise to the top, which saw him make the jump from non-league Fleetwood Town to Leicester when they were in the Championship, and it was a move that kickstarted his career, which would eventually make him a household name.

Vardy is still playing in the Championship right now, turning out for Burnley, and is undoubtedly one of the most famous names in the league.

Walker is a teammate of Vardy’s at Turf Moor, and he is a player who has enjoyed a glittering career at the highest level.

During his time with Man City, the right-back won six Premier League titles, a Champions League and numerous domestic trophies. Walker was integral to City’s success under Pep Guardiola, and is in the discussion as the best right-back the league has seen.

When you add in 96 England caps, Walker has had a remarkable career, which started with Sheffield United in the Championship.

Many people consider Cole as the best left-back England have ever had, with the Arsenal academy graduate winning over 100 caps for the Three Lions, which is a fantastic achievement.

During his club career with the Gunners and Chelsea, Cole won every honour possible, which included lifting the Champions League with the Blues after beating Bayern Munich on their own patch in 2012.

Cole was a superb one-vs-one defender, and whilst he spent the majority of his career at the top, he ended up at Derby County, and whilst he didn’t make a huge impact at Pride Park, having a player of that calibre at the club would’ve benefited the younger players.

Bellingham is one of the most famous footballers on the planet right now, with the midfielder starring for Real Madrid and England.

But, it all started for the Stourbridge-born Bellingham at Birmingham City, who are a club that are still close to his heart. He broke through at Blues as a 16-year-old, and it became apparent very quickly that they had a special talent on their hands.

At 23, Bellingham still has so much more to offer, and there’s every chance that he could go on to become the most famous footballer on this list, as he will fancy his chances of winning the Ballon d’Or, as well as aiming for more success with Real Madrid, and leading England to a major trophy.

Terry is another Premier League legend, with the defender among the best centre-backs to have played at the top level in English football during his time with Chelsea.

He won five Premier League titles, five FA Cups, three League Cups and a Champions League in a brilliant career, with Terry also representing England 78 times, many of which were as captain.

Even though Terry is associated with Chelsea, he ended his playing career at Aston Villa in the Championship, with his final game a play-off final loss to Fulham at Wembley.

Bale is a legend of Welsh football, having been the driving force behind what has been their best period in the past decade, where they qualified for major tournaments and reached the semi-final of Euro 2016.

On the club stage, Bale was part of a Real Madrid team that dominated in Europe, and he ended his career having won the Champions League five times, which is an outstanding achievement.

It all started for Bale with Southampton, though, where he had one full breakout season before joining Spurs.

The ex-Man Utd forward is one of the best players that England have produced, and he is another player on the list that won every honour available during his club career.

Rooney also won 120 caps for England, and he was the Three Lions’ record goalscorer before he was beaten by Harry Kane, so he was a key figure for both club and country for the chunk of his time as a player.

The attacker was another player who ended his career in the Championship, with Rooney joining Derby County under Phillip Cocu, who he would then replace as head coach, to give him his first taste of management.

Who is the most famous footballer you've seen in the Championship? Let us know in the comments below.

Kane may not have the trophy cabinet of many on this list, but as the only Ballon d’Or winner, we feel he has to go in as number one.

The striker is the all-time England record goalscorer and appearance maker, and he is now picking up silverware on a regular basis with Bayern Munich, having undoubtedly established himself as one of the best players in the world in the past few years.

That recognition as number one on the planet arrived earlier this year, and it capped off an incredible journey for Kane, who turned out for Millwall and Leicester in the Championship during loan spells earlier in his career, and for Leyton Orient in League One.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#2070. Malo Gusto’s Kante Lesson Gives Chelsea A £75m Xabi Alonso Decision

Malo Gusto’s World Cup has suddenly become more than a France subplot for Chelsea. It is now a live assessment of whether Xabi Alonso inherits a right-back worth protecting, reshaping or trading at the peak of his market.

Chelsea’s own interview with Gusto this week underlined the human part of that equation. The 23-year-old spoke about learning from N’Golo Kante, calling the former Blue one of the best midfielders France have produced and stressing the value of his example on and off the pitch.

That matters because Kante is not just a nostalgic reference point. He remains the standard Chelsea supporters still use when judging humility, intensity and reliability in a high-pressure dressing room.

For Gusto, those qualities arrive at a decisive moment. Reports around the player’s future claim Chelsea value him at around £75million, with the imminent Marco Palestra deal creating a more crowded full-back picture.

That number looks aggressive, but the logic is clear. Gusto is young, capped by France, under contract, Premier League-tested and capable of playing in several defensive structures.

🚨🚨| NEW: Chelsea are open to selling Malo Gusto this summer, with his agent already in 𝐓𝐀𝐋𝐊𝐒 with Manchester City and Inter. Chelsea will only sell if their valuation is met.{@siphillipssport} pic.twitter.com/vNR2bWud9F

The easiest reading of Gusto’s Kante comments is sentimental. It should not be.

For Alonso, who officially begins work on July 1, the important detail is what those comments say about the player Chelsea have been developing.

Gusto has not always looked completely settled at Stamford Bridge. His best games have carried thrust, speed and recovery power, while his less convincing spells have raised questions about final-ball quality and defensive concentration.

That uncertainty is exactly why the next coach matters.

Alonso’s previous teams have leaned heavily on wide players who can receive under pressure, attack space early and still protect the back line when possession breaks down. Gusto has the athletic base for that job.

The test is whether his decision-making can be refined enough to make him a structural piece rather than a rotation asset.

That is where the Kante reference lands with force. Chelsea do not need Gusto to imitate Kante’s position. They need him to absorb the same professional standard: repeat actions, clean defensive choices, no wasted emotion and total commitment to the collective rhythm.

The Marco Palestra deal changes the right side of Chelsea’s squad immediately. Read Chelsea has already examined how Palestra’s arrival offers a tactical clue over Alonso’s defensive plans, and that pressure is now sharpened by market noise around Gusto.

Chelsea can frame the situation in two ways.

One is profit-led. If a club comes close to the reported £75million level, selling a player signed from Lyon for a much lower fee becomes a powerful PSR lever.

The other is football-led. If Alonso sees Gusto as a high-upside wing-back who fits his model, selling him just as the coaching environment becomes more suitable would carry long-term risk.

The complication is Reece James. The captain’s fitness issues, including his current England hamstring concern, mean Chelsea still need genuine right-sided depth.

Palestra may be part of the future, but Gusto is already part of the present. Chelsea have too often needed emergency solutions in that area to treat proven depth lightly.

That is why Read Chelsea’s recent look at James awaiting hamstring scan results matters in this debate. Right-back remains one of the most talented areas of the squad, but also one of the least straightforward.

This is why Gusto’s France rhythm is more valuable than a simple tournament diary entry. Chelsea are watching a player operate inside an elite international camp, learn from a club legend and handle a public transfer valuation that can change his status overnight.

Alonso’s first decision does not have to be final, but it does have to be clear.

If Gusto stays, he needs a defined role early in pre-season and a pathway that makes sense alongside Palestra and James. If Chelsea sell, they need to do it at a number that justifies weakening one of the few squad areas where youth, speed and top-level experience already overlap.

Gusto’s Kante lesson, then, is not just a feel-good Chelsea connection. It is a reminder of the standard Alonso must demand before deciding whether £75million is a price to accept or a warning sign that Chelsea should hold firm.

#2068. Senegal Knockout Tie Gives Chelsea A Double Xabi Alonso Audit

Chelsea’s World Cup watch has moved beyond simple minutes management.

Senegal’s Round-of-32 meeting with Belgium now gives Xabi Alonso a live read on two very different development tracks.

Nicolas Jackson’s attacking authority is the immediate question. Mamadou Sarr’s defensive readiness is the longer-term one.

Chelsea confirmed that Senegal kept their knockout hopes alive with a 5-0 win over Iraq, with Jackson featuring from the bench.

Senegal have since moved into the knockouts, where they face Belgium in Seattle on Wednesday 1 July.

Jackson and Sarr travel into that game with contrasting club questions attached. Both still carry clear Chelsea relevance.

Sarr has not been the loudest Chelsea story of the tournament.

That may actually make this test more useful.

The 20-year-old is still moving through the awkward stage between prospect, squad option and saleable BlueCo asset.

Knockout football against Belgium can sharpen that picture quickly.

The timing is awkward in the best possible way for Chelsea. Alonso steps into a squad with expensive centre-backs, academy-trained options and a board still comfortable using the market aggressively.

A disciplined Sarr performance would not end that search. It would give the recruitment team a stronger internal benchmark before committing another major fee.

Chelsea need defenders who can hold a high line, cover wide channels and still pass through pressure. Belgium should ask those questions more directly than most group-stage opponents.

The context matters. Chelsea’s recall note recorded that Sarr returned from Strasbourg after 18 appearances across Ligue 1 and the Conference League.

The club also noted that he had already earned his first Senegal cap.

That is a different profile from an academy player being carried by reputation alone.

There is a statistical base behind the interest too. When Chelsea completed the deal, beIN SPORTS noted that Sarr made 27 Ligue 1 appearances in his first Strasbourg season.

He helped them keep 10 clean sheets. He also produced a team-high 20 blocks and made 25 interceptions.

Those numbers explain why this Belgium game is not just a sentimental World Cup subplot.

Alonso’s Chelsea defence is already crowded with Levi Colwill, Wesley Fofana, Trevoh Chalobah and external targets still orbiting the plan.

ReadChelsea has already looked at why Colwill’s recovery story gives Alonso a defensive test. Sarr’s value is different.

He is still being evaluated as a physical, long-range defensive project.

Jackson’s role changes the editorial weight of the tie.

Chelsea’s striker picture has been messy for long enough. Any high-pressure international performance now carries wider meaning.

ReadChelsea has already framed the forward’s tournament as a live Senegal striker audit for Chelsea.

Belgium should stress both Chelsea questions at once.

Jackson has to offer penalty-box threat and transition security. Sarr, if trusted, has to defend space against a technically cleaner opponent.

He also has to show whether his recovery pace and frame translate under tournament pressure.

Sarr’s own mentality profile is worth noting. In a Chelsea World Cup Q&A, he named Lionel Messi, Sadio Mane and Paul Pogba as his tournament heroes.

His answer on Pogba focused on leadership and group mentality.

That lands neatly with the exact question Chelsea now need answered. Is there enough presence to go with the physical tools?

This is why Belgium feels like a pathway check rather than a routine World Cup watch item.

Chelsea do not need Sarr to solve the defence in July. They need clearer evidence on whether he belongs in Alonso’s first pre-season group.

He could need another loan. He could also become part of the club’s centre-back market arithmetic.

For Jackson, the question is more immediate. For Sarr, it is more structural.

Together, Senegal’s knockout tie gives Chelsea a rare clean look at two players on opposite ends of the same squad-building argument.

Who can help now, and who is worth protecting for later?

#2066. Jamie Carragher names Man Utd Star who impressed him against Leeds

Shumail Sajid writes about Manchester United for Read Man Utd and Crystal Palace for Read Crystal Palace, with occasional pieces on other Premier League clubs. He has also written for FanSided's Red Devils Dispatch, Yardbarker, Anfield Central and The Sports Side.

Manchester United had a difficult evening once again as they were held to a 1-1 draw at Leeds United. Pressure mounts on Michael Carrick as United have just 7 points from 7 games.

Manchester United took the lead through Bryan Mbeumo in the first half, with the forward finishing Youri Tielemans’ excellent cross from the right. However, the visitors couldn’t hold on to their advantage as Dominic Calvert-Lewin equalised for Leeds United from a corner.

The draw extended United’s frustrating run of results, leaving Michael Carrick still searching for the consistency his side need.

Carragher, though, believes there were positives to take from the trip, particularly one performance at the back.

Jamie Carragher has singled out Harry Maguire for praise after Manchester United drew 1-1 with Leeds United at Elland Road on Sunday.

Speaking on Sky Sports, the former Liverpool defender admitted that picking up a point at Elland Road was not necessarily a bad result in isolation, even if United’s recent form made it feel like a missed opportunity.

“Going away to Leeds is going to be tricky for any team except for Manchester City and Arsenal at the moment,” Carragher said.

“A lot of teams will take a point at Leeds this season but the problem for Manchester United is the results have been so poor that they need to start winning games so it almost feels like two points dropped.”

Carragher then turned his attention to Maguire, who he felt played a major role in keeping United in the game when Leeds began to push for a winner.

“But in isolation, getting a point at Leeds is a decent result. I thought Harry Maguire was fantastic, especially in the second half.”

Leeds United grew into the contest after Calvert-Lewin brought them level, putting United under pressure during the closing stages. Carragher felt Maguire’s efforts in defence helped prevent the visitors from falling apart.

“After Leeds got that goal back there was a stage of the game where it felt like Man United could go under, but Maguire at the back held it together for them. He was fantastic.”

The result may feel like another opportunity missed for Carrick, but Maguire’s performance gave United something positive to take away from Elland Road.

#2065. Bradford City takeover: Everything we know right now

Bradford City are being linked to a potential takeover by a Thai-based consortium, so here's a round-up of the latest on whether this move might come off.

The international break couldn't have come at a better time for Bradford City.

Following an exceptional start to the season, the departure of manager Graham Alexander to Preston North End at the start of October hit the club hard, and they went into the break with just one win from their last six league matches and having slipped from the top of the League One table to eighth place, having replaced Alexander with the former Wycombe Wanderers manager Michael Duff.

But losing Alexander may not even be the biggest change to be coming to Bradford City this season. It's been rumoured that a Thai-based consortium are considering launching a bid to buy the club from current owner Stefan Rupp, with the group having been attracted by the club's recent upward trajectory and potential, given the size of attendances they were attracting, even while the team was misfiring in League Two.

This isn't the first time since Rupp purchased the club in 2016 that there has been an attempt to wrest Bradford City from his control, so here's a round-up of what's been said about ongoing reported interest in buying them, and what it could mean for a club who previously slipped from the Premier League to League Two in just six years, between 2001 and 2007.

A report from journalist Alan Nixon on Sunday morning has reopened conjecture that the Bradford City owner Stefan Rupp could be set to sell the club after ten years of ownership. Nixon confirmed on his Patreon that "Bradford City are a surprise target for a Thai-based group" who have been considering buying into the EFL.

Nixon confirmed that the prospective bidders have shown interest in buying a club before, and that, "Bradford could be for sale at the right price and the Thais, who have an intermediary with inside knowledge, are considering an official offer."

Do you think Bradford City would be better off under new ownership? Let us know in the comments below!

But before anything else, any new owners will have to get a takeover past Rupp, and that might not be completely straightforward. The German has been reported to be more open to selling since the club were promoted from League Two in 2025, with The Athletic's Matt Slater reporting in March 2026 that, "Rupp has been listening to offers for years but has showing a bit more leg ever since last season’s promotion."

Rupp has, however, said in the past that he won't sell up to just anybody. In 2021, he rejected an offer from the US cryptocurrency investors WAGMI United. They instead turned their attention to Crawley Town but, since completing their takeover of the Sussex-based club in April 2022, Crawley's position has waned considerably, with the Red Devils currently propping up the rest of the EFL and six points from safety.

Rumours that Bradford City could be sold have provoked a strong reaction from fans of the club, so here's a selection of what they've had to say.

This poll of fans showed a majority of those who voted being against any takeover of their club:

While this fan doesn't believe that these rumours should be a surprise to anybody:

This fan is concerned over what's happened at several other clubs who've come under far eastern ownership:

And this fan believes that Stefan Rupp has already demonstrated that he is the owner that Bradford City need:

Their recent slump in League One notwithstanding, the direction of travel that Bradford City have undertaken over the last couple of seasons makes them a prime target for those seeking to buy into the English game.

For years, it felt as though the Bantams had everything bar the team. They had a stadium which is fit for Premier League football, and attendances were extremely healthy, even when the team wasn't performing especially well in League Two. On top of this, being the only professional football club in a city of half a million people gives the opportunity for further growth, should they continue to rise through the divisions.

Under Alexander, the team was finally successful, winning promotion back to League One in 2025 following an absence of six years, and their first season back hinted that the Bantams weren't done either, with the team finishing in a highly creditable fourth place before losing 2-0 on aggregate to Bolton Wanderers in the semi-finals of the play-offs.

But there is one word in Alan Nixon's report which may cause Bradford fans to worry a little about the nature of the group who are now being linked with the club. Nixon described this consortium as "speculators", and that will raise concerns about the motives of this group among some.

There isn't anywhere near enough detail about this group to be able to draw too many inferences about their intentions for the club, though it's previously been reported that they are connected to the former owners of Oxford United. But "speculators" is a loaded word, and there may be concern over whether they will have their own interests at heart or those of the club should they take over.

And when speaking to the Bradford Telegraph & Argus at the end of June, Rupp confirmed that, "You get requests from time to time but they are tyre kickers, people without money, wannabe football club owners, or people you simply don't like," and that, "I'm the keeper of the keys and I would never hand it over to somebody where I have the impression he can't do any better."

The sale price, should it be the same as it was reported to be earlier in 2026, would be unlikely to be too much of a sticking point. The Athletic's report in March suggested that £10 million could be enough to persuade him to sell, with Bradford owning neither their own ground nor their training ground, but such a sum could still only be considered a drop in the ocean, were the club to ascend to the Championship or beyond.

Still in the FA Cup, and with an EFL Cup quarter-final at Manchester City to look forward to in the middle of December, Bradford City remain in a better condition on the pitch than they have been for years, and the big irony of their current position is that this very success may push up their sale price. Stefan Rupp has said before that he will only sell the club to the right buyer, but the true test of his principles may come when the rumours cease and concrete offers start to land on his desk.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#2064. Newcastle scrape past Millwall to extend Jaissle’s unbeaten start

Joe Willock’s deft finish ensured Newcastle United survived a tough test against Millwall to keep their excellent run in the Carabao Cup intact.

This competition had been fruitful for Newcastle under former manager Eddie Howe and although this match was hard work – as well as hard to watch at times – his successor Matthias Jaissle guided them through a difficult trip to south-east London.

He called it “job done,” and that was pretty much all it was. “We needed patience on one hand, but also to be passionate and tough. We had the chance [to score] and took it,” he said.

Newcastle have reached the semi-finals of this competition three times in the last four years, but struggled to get any sort of tempo going against their Championship opponents.

You could argue the winning goal came against the run of play late in the second half, moments after Millwall substitute Taïryk Arconte had smashed a low shot against the post.

"Livramento had a NIGHTMARE, he's so lucky" 😨Millwall were INCHES away from taking the lead against Newcastle 🤏 pic.twitter.com/X26aiTL432

Given they were missing 13 players because of injury, this was a brave display from Alex Neil’s side. They frustrated Newcastle for more than an hour, nullifying their attack, to the point where Jaissle’s team looked as though they had run out of ideas.

That was until Lewis Hall combined with Matias Fernandez-Pardo down the left and his drilled cross found Willock who cleverly used the angle to pass the ball into the net. Willock has been rejuvenated under Jaissle. He looked certain to be sold this summer but is now starting regularly under a new manager in the number 10 role his system demands. It has been a nice redemption arc for the former Arsenal academy graduate.

Moments after Millwall hit the post, Joe Willock strikes to put Newcastle in front! ⚽️ pic.twitter.com/rSB8yV6NRO

The victory is all that matters and extends Jaissle’s unbeaten start to five games. Given he arrived just three weeks before the start of the season, that deserves praise even if it is obvious there is a lot of work to be done to improve their offensive play.

Playing in their lilac, or should that be Parma-violet, third kit for the first time, Newcastle looked off colour in the first half. Even though Jaissle named a strong team packed with experience of English cup ties, they struggled to overpower Millwall.

There were a few half-chances as Willock forced a save and Jacob Murphy fired over. There was a header missed from a corner by Sven Botman, which should have hit the target and Yoane Wissa also mistimed his jump after finding space for another header.

Millwall’s two centre-backs, Jake Cooper and Caleb Taylor were immense, flinging themselves in the way of every shot and clearing every loose ball that came into their vicinity. Given their injuries, this was a performance full of fight and defiance from the home side.

However, there was also an absence of quality in the final third from Newcastle, the same lack of cohesion and incision that was apparent at home to Bournemouth last weekend and in the first half away at Tottenham Hotspur.

It meant Millwall were happy to play for set-pieces close to the Newcastle box and Taylor got in front of his marker, flashing a header wide of the post.

That lacklustre first half meant Jaissle’s side had mustered just five shots on target in five halves of football since the 3-2 win over West Bromwich Albion in the previous round of the Carabao Cup.

Millwall started the second period like a side sensing Newcastle were vulnerable. A thunderbolt from Jenson Metcalfe, after the visitors had struggled to clear two crosses, almost gave them a spectacular lead.

Newcastle saw lots of the ball. Millwall were happy enough to let them have it given how little they were hurting them.

So much of Newcastle’s play was slow and cumbersome. Their set-piece delivery was also largely inept.

Neil’s side retained a threat and came so close to taking the lead when, not for the first time, a long ball forward caught the Newcastle defence out of shape and Tino Livramento’s mistake allowed Arconte to run clear and hit the post from a tight angle.

Well in, @Joewillock! 💪 pic.twitter.com/5a8G7lzD3H

Speaking after the game, Millwall manager Alex Neil said: “I’m very proud, I don’t think we deserved to lose that game.

“We had some good moments, and we got done by a bit of sucker punch at the end. But I’m very proud of the lads.”

As for their injury problems, he added: “I didn’t bring the teenagers on as a token gesture, I need to keep the first-team players fit. We’re really at bare bones.

But we beat Bolton at the weekend, got a couple of defeats before that but we started the season really well and once we get everybody back, we’ll be in good shape.”

With the first of the 16 teams through tonight, the draw won’t take place until most of the teams have played next week.

The draw will be shown on Sky Sports on Wednesday 16th Sept, after Manchester United play Brighton. Man City vs Norwich will be the only game outstanding then.

The third round had to be spread over two weeks as the nine Premier League sides in UEFA competitions entered the tournament in this round, as the same time as their Champions League and Europa League fixtures began. To avoid clubs facing clashes, the EFL split the fixtures across the two gameweeks.

Still got some more post-match to come for you, but we’ve got scores from all our matches tonight now:

From the Champions League, Man City held out against Porto to win 2-0.

“I think we had a lot of chances in the first half, and we went in a half-time saying we need to  take our chances, so I’m glad we came out in the second half and we did,” said Willock after the match.

“100% [the competition is important], we’ve won it before so it’s very important to us, but every game is important to us. Especially with a new coach and a lot of new players, we wanted to start the new season well. I think we started really well and we need to continue and this was a big game in keeping that momentum.”

"We said at half-time we NEED to take our chances"Lewis Hall and Joe Willock react to Newcastle's win over Millwall 🎙️ pic.twitter.com/NDF3laD8nT

Take a look at the match-winner from Joe Willock:

Moments after Millwall hit the post, Joe Willock strikes to put Newcastle in front! ⚽️ pic.twitter.com/rSB8yV6NRO

The goal came minutes after Millwall were inches away from taking the lead themselves, as Arconte was denied by the post:

"Livramento had a NIGHTMARE, he's so lucky" 😨Millwall were INCHES away from taking the lead against Newcastle 🤏 pic.twitter.com/X26aiTL432

We’ll be bringing you more from the post-match now.

Joe Willock has done enough for Newcastle to reach the fourth round and keep the travelling fans singing all the way back to the North-East.

It won’t go down in history as the greatest Carabao fixture, but Newcastle found a way to keep their momentum going and give Matthias Jaissle a win on his cup debut.

Newcastle aren’t taking any risks as Hornicek sends the ball long, and the players keep looking to send the ball down-field.

Seconds to go now. Marschall sends it long for one last effort, but it is cleared out of the box...

Willock has come off now for Newcastle’s own teenager, Sean Steur. A few more minutes and the man now on the bench with have done enough to send his side through to the next round.

We’re into the final minutes as Millwall are throwing everything at this.

Millwall are not out of this yet, as Neghli comes down the left side, twisting his way into the box past his defender – but having done the hard work, his shot flashes low across goal.

Some more changes, as Ramsey comes off for Newcastle, replaced by Lewis Miley.

A double change for the hosts as Dykes and Kelly come off for Regan Monty and Alfie Massey – the former just 15 years old.

Seconds later, another teenager takes to the pitch for Millwall as Osei-Tutu is replaced by 17-year-old Tristan Parkes.

Newcastle almost have another! From the sublime to the ridiculous, as Willock makes another run, this time down the left, and passes the ball onto the edge of the box where Elanga meets it in space. He lets it run, before taking his shot, but it is straight to Marschall.

Finally Newcastle have their breakthrough! They punish Millwall as Fernandez-Pardo feeds Hall on the left, who cuts inside and slips the ball across goal, finding Willock to redirect the ball to slot it home.

Marschall releases Arconte with a long ball and he turns Livramento to find huge amounts of space on the right side. He races into the box and takes a shot from close range, aiming for his near post, but is denied by the woodwork and the rebound hits the seated Hornicek. The keeper is lucky to not concede an own goal, as the ball bounces up and over his leg.

Issoufou again racing down the right side, before cutting inside and taking a shot with his left foot. Hall, who has been so crucial in the Newcastle attack, throws himself at the shot, and it flies high for Hornicek to collect.

Replays show that González, who Millwall players claimed had handled the ball earlier, leant down to clear with his shoulder.

Issoufou sends a great ball in for Millwall from the right side, but it is cleared by a Newcastle player, accompanied by cries for handball.

The game is opening up now as Newcastle make a run of their own, with Willock creating an opening for Elanga to take the ball to the edge of the box, before Taylor slides in to block his shot.

Millwall could absolutely win this with a smash-and-grab with less than 20 minutes to go. They are pushing for it but are lacking some attacking quality to finish the job.

From six shots they’ve had two on target, compared to Newcastle’s three on target from 20.

Fernandez-Pardo gets his first look at the ball, making a very quick run down across the centre of the field to the left side, but Osei-Tutu stays with him and takes him all the way to the back line before giving up a corner.

Elanga takes the corner, punched away by the keeper but no one goes to finish the job and Newcastle get another corner.

Metcalfe, who had his red card overturned this week, is the first player to go in the book for a mistimed challenge on Ramsey.

Just a reminder that there is no extra time, so if we’re all square after 90 minutes, it’s straight to a penalty shoot-out.

Willock gets the ball on the edge of the area and passes it on a quick turn to Barnes just inside the box, but there was not much on his shot and Marschall collects easily.

Double change now for Newcastle as Wissa and Murphy come off, replaced by Elanga and Fernandez-Pardo as Jaissle looks for pace. Schar is handed the armband.

Free kick for Newcastle, right on the corner of the box. Murphy takes, but it hits the wall 10 feet away, and bounces straight back to him. His cross into the box is headed out, and for all the opportunities Newcastle have created, they are yet to find the breakthrough.

We’ve also had a double change for Millwall as Esse and Lovelace have come off, replaced by Issoufou and Arconte.

What colour would you describe this Newcastle away shirt? They look like the sweets Purple Violet to me. Although would you call it an all Lilac number?

It’s the first time they have worn their third kit. Not sure whether I like it or not.  Shame The Den isn’t a sell out although I’m told tickets were priced at £31 and Millwall have a lot of injuries too.

Newcastle get another corner after a run from Willock. The delivery from Hall creates a good amount of confusion in the box and Marschall isn’t sure whether to stay on his line or come out to punch it away. From within the bodies, Wissa tries to get a shot off from close range but it bounces and the keeper easily collects.

González commits another foul, pulling down Esse, to give Millwall another free kick from 40 yards out.

The ball meets Taylor at the back post, but he meets it in the air and can’t quite direct it either into goal or back into the six-yard box, so it goes out for a Newcastle goal kick.

Another half chance for Millwall as Dykes feeds Kelly on the right side, who runs into the box and gets caught between passing the ball in and taking the shot, with the ball going high over the box.

Another great challenge from Osei-Tutu as Willock makes a run into the box, but is brought down by a well-timed tackle from the right-back.

The corner from Hall is better, but headed out and cleared.

Barnes again with space on the left side and he sends a ball fizzing low across the box to the far post but Neghli is able to lean on Murphy to stop him making contact.

Scramble for Newcastle as the ball is sent by Dykes to Neghli free at the far post, who puts the ball into a very dangerous area just in front of goal and everyone jumps on. Newcastle get to it first, managing to clear it from the goal mouth. It is cleared outside the box and it bounces to unmarked Metcalfe, who takes a thunderous shot, putting his laces through the ball but he is unable to keep it down and it goes over the bar.

Despite Alex Neil’s premonitions, no changes for Millwall at the break.

Right-back change for Newcastle, as Dedic comes off and Tino Livramento comes on.

The earlier kick-offs of the Carabao third round have just started their second periods, but here are the latest scores:

Aston Villa won their opening Champions League fixture 3-2 against Club Brugge, while Man City are still goalless against Porto, which you can follow with our live blog here

And that’s the last action of the half, as just one minute was added on and that was taken up by Newcastle’s corner.

Nothing separates the two sides at the half, thought the visitors have dominated in terms of possession and chances.

Millwall have held fast and will be happy to be finishing the half level. We may see some changes from them after the break.

The game is opening up before half-time, and Newcastle go again with Hall and Barnes. Osei-Tutu does well to wait before going in to block Barnes’s shot and send the ball behind for another Newcastle corner.

The delivery is once again poor, but Schar is pulled down inside the box by Taylor and is furious that nothing was given. There’s no VAR so there’s no review to consider – but looking at replays, Millwall were very lucky to get away with that foul.

Cooper makes a perfect pass down the left sideline, allowing Neghli to find space and forcing Newcastle to clear it away fo a Millwall corner.

The ball in is promising but Hornicek gets to it and punches it away, but the hosts keep the pressure on.

Baggott floats another ball across the box towards the right back post, but Hornicek easily collects the ball as Neghli can’t quite connect.

Newcastle moving the ball well again across midfield and it comes to Schar, who runs into space and gets a low shot away, around 40 yards out. It  takes a slight deflection on its way, going just wide of the post.

González is not having his best night and makes a silly foul against Dykes on the sideline, giving the hosts another set piece. The swinging ball in is not nearly as good as last time, and only reaches the first man, Newcastle’s Ramsey.

Millwall get a free kick, and the delivery is good, allowing Taylor to connect on the header inside the box. He beats Hornicek but the header rolls just wide of the post, to the groans of the home fans.

Hall goes short with the corner and Dedic has lots of time to cross the ball in from the right. It’s headed away but Millwall can’t break on the counter.

That sums up the game pretty well: not much finishing quality from Newcastle but Millwall not creating much from their limited spells of possession.

Newcastle pushing again. Another ball pulled back by Barnes finds Ramsey at the top of the box, and his ball in connects with Wissa. Newcastle’s captain can’t head it in the right direction though and Millwall survive again.

The spell of pressure results in another corner for the visitors – and now we’re getting some pushing in the six-yard box.

I think Millwall have done well. They have limited Newcastle to half chances and the odd set piece threat. They have made things really difficult for the visitors, crowding them out of space on the edge of the area.

When the home side have advanced up the pitch the Newcastle defence has not looked particularly secure.

As we reach the half-hour mark, Newcastle have 10 shots to Millwall’s one, though they sit one apiece on shots on target.

Esse gets caught on his heels as Hall pulls a long ball back on the left, and in the crowd at the top of the box Willock takes a shot, pulling it wide – cheers from the home crowd again.

First piece of good attacking play from Millwall as Neghli and Baggott work on the overlap. Baggott lofts a high ball to the back post, where Dykes gets a foot on it on the volley, but he can’t quite get over it and it’s easily picked up by Hornicek.

Barnes and Ramsey combine again down the left, with the midfielder trying to feed Barnes on his run. The pass has too much on it though, and as it runs out the back it’s met with jeers from the home fans for a goal kick.

Wissa breaks away down the centre of the field, with Barnes on his left, using him as a decoy. Wissa takes the shot though and it is blocked by a sliding defender.

Newcastle hit 20 minutes in with 68 per cent possession but nothing to show yet for their efforts. You feel like it will only be a matter of time though.

Another Newcastle corner, swung in well and Botman comes charging in, beating cooper to a free header. The defender heads it over the bar and holds his head in his hands. The visitors could definitely be a goal up by now.

Hall’s free-kick is met by the first man Metcalfe who heads it away to atone for his foul and Newcastle remain stymied.

Millwall will have expected Newcastle to dominate the ball but they are really pushing for an opener, especially down the left side with Barnes and Hall.

Again, Newcastle coming down the wings, this time on the left. Esse picks the ball up but loses it and Willock picks it up and takes a shot on his right foot with good power but sends it straight at Marschall. The debut keeper parries it away and it’s cleared by a  Millwall header.

Willock comes down the left soon after and is fouled by Metcalfe to get a free kick in a good spot outside the box.

Murphy gets a shot off after Dedic picks up a long ball on the right side and crosses it back towards the middle of the field. Murphy gets on it and takes the shot inside the box off his left foot but it sails over the bar.

González gives the ball away cheaply and Metcalfe picks it up, but unable to move it forward.

Newcastle will need to make sure they don’t get complacent in defence.

Millwall having a spell of possession, the counter-attack looking like their best option but as they move down the right hand side, Lovelace makes a late challenge to get the ball back and fouls Wissa.

Newcastle advancing, with Dedic and Ramsey moving the ball across midfield. Barnes gets the ball on the left of the box, and his ball is in knocked out and Newcastle get the first corner of the game.

Nothing comes of it as it is sent in high and long over the box.

Fair to say both teams are settling, but Millwall try and create a chance with Lovelace, though it’s intercepted. Dykes takes a bit of a knock and is slow to get up.

Here we go in south London, and Millwall get us started.

Just a reminder of the teams starting today:

Starting XI: Filip Marschall; Jordi Osei-Tutu, Caleb Taylor, Jake Cooper, Elkan Baggott; Lyndon Dykes, Jenson Metcalfe; Camiel Neghli, Daniel Kelly, Romain Esse; Zak Lovelace

Substitutes: Regan Monty, Tristan Parkes, Sacha Vieira, George Beaumont, Yanis Issoufou, George Evans, Taïryk Arconte, Alfie Massey, Zak Sturge

Starting XI: Lukás Hornícek; Lewis Hall, Fabian Schär, Amar Dedic, Sven Botman; Jacob Murphy, Nico González; Jacob Ramsey, Harvey Barnes, Joe Willock; Yoane Wissa

Substitutes: Tino Livramento, Anthony Elanga, Malick Thiaw, Nick Pope, Lewis Miley, Bazoumana Touré, Matias Fernandez-Pardo, Aladji Bamba, Sean Steur

The teams are coming out of the tunnel, and both home and away fans in the Den are already in loud voice. Kick off on the way!

"We've tried to find the right balance" ⚖️Matthias Jaissle on his team selection for tonight's match with Millwall ⚫️ pic.twitter.com/kiRRxAgLk8

We’re just a few minutes away from kick off in south London, but Bournemouth have scored the first goal of the third round, with Ryan Christie putting his side ahead against Lincoln.

Alex Neil has not minced his words over his squad’s injury crisis. His team is down 13 players, which the coach says has “definitely forced” his hand in terms of squad rotation.

Playing two matches a week in the “relentless” Championship has turned his squad selection into a “needs must scenario” and he even admitted he “may need to make a couple of changes at half-time depending on how the game goes”

Matthias Jaissle is clearly taking this competition seriously and having started the league well, he is still trying to get the fans onside and create momentum for his team.

At the same time, Telegraph Sport have reported that Ross Wilson, the sporting director, has warned there will have to be more departures in future windows. Having lost Alexander Isak, Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimarães in 12 months, there will be yet be more upheaval.

You can read Luke Edwards’ full story on that here

The Premier League teams playing in European competitions enter the EFL Cup in this round, with all 16 fixtures being played over five match days. As well as tonight’s games there will be:

Fleetwood Town vs Sheffield United (7.45pm)

*all kick-off at 8pm, unless stated otherwise

Newcastle have named a strong side – probably the strongest they could field when factoring in senior players needing game time – to take on Millwall in the Carabao Cup.

Jacob Ramsey impressed coming off the bench against Bournemouth last weekend and manager Matthias Jaissle refused to sanction winger Jacob Murphy’s transfer to Nottingham Forest late in the window. Both deserve a chance to impress from the start.

Veteran centre back Fabian Schar comes in for Malick Thiaw, but those are the only three changes from the side that drew with Bournemouth.

Jaissle insisted he would take the competition seriously and the teamsheet proves it, but it also raises questions about some of Newcastle’s summer recruitment.

Bazoumana Toure cost £42m but was withdrawn at half time in the win over West Brom in the previous round, which means Harvey Barnes does not get a rest. That’s a lot of money to spend on a winger who has not looked Premier League ready so far.

Aladji Bamba, a £30m signing from Monaco, has not started a game yet and has been an unused substitute since the opening game against Liverpool. He remains on the bench.

Even Sean Steur, who has looked good since his summer move from Ajax, cannot dislodge another more recent arrival in former Manchester City midfielder Nico González.

Having made a total of eight new signings in a much-vaunted summer rebuild, Jaissle only started three of them against Bournemouth and only two start tonight at The Den.

Early days but this was one of the main reasons Eddie Howe quit – he did not think the likes of Toure, Steur and Bamba were ready to play first team football.

The visitors have arrived in south London

We've made it to South East London 👋 pic.twitter.com/nh8Fpa37xT

We’re bringing you the action from the pick of tonight’s EFL Cup games but there are also four games kicking off at 7.45pm:

The Champions League also returns tonight and you can follow along with both our blogs:

Aston Villa are currently 3-1 up against Club Brugge in Belgium – follow the action here

Manchester City will face Porto at 8.00pm – our live blog has just gone live here with the team news from both sides

Yoane Wissa takes the captain’s armband tonight, while Jacob Ramsey starts up front after scoring a late equaliser against Bournemouth on Saturday

Your Mags at Millwall ✊ pic.twitter.com/zfnHgTlWgh

Keeper Filip Marschall is making his debut while Jensen Metcalfe is back in the squad after his red card against Bolton was overturned on appeal

How your Lions line-up tonight 🔢 pic.twitter.com/wEp6qLIz4Y

Welcome to tonight’s live coverage of Millwall vs Newcastle United, as the Geordies travel to south London for the third round of the Carabao Cup.

Newcastle held off West Brom in their second-round match, with Harvey Barnes scoring two second-half goals to see his side through. It was a mighty comeback, after Isaac Price scored early to stun the crowd at St James’ Park. Bazoumana Toure equalised for Matthias Jaissle’s side just before half-time, and Barnes, his replacement in the second half, put them ahead minutes after the restart. West Brom pulled it back to 2-2 with a penalty converted by Price after Lewis Hall was deemed to have handled the ball in the box, but Barnes got his second just nine minutes from full-time and the hosts were able to see out the match to progress.

Alex Neil’s Millwall have reached round three via a 0-1 win over Cambridge United, following a penalty shoot-out in the first round to beat QPR. They come into this tie with a squad stretched thin, as they have been hit with an injury crisis a month into the new season. Millwall have confirmed that they will be without Casper De Norre, Josh Coburn, Tristan Crama, Alfie Doughty, Mathis Servais, Ryan Leonard, Mihailo Ivanovic, Lukas Jensen and Luke Cundle.

Both sides sit seventh in their respective leagues, with Millwall on a record of three wins and two losses this season, while Newcastle remain unbeaten (two draws and a win).
